attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. He relays Bloomberg but endorses it, saying he had confirmed it himself.

semantics.note: Keeps the three parts: OpenAI out of the expansion, the 'past the first two buildings' scope, and the delay against the mid-2026 target. It drops the 'Bloomberg reported' framing, which doesn't change the result.

contract.note: Reading the parenthetical as buildings three to eight is the ordinary reading. His own context, which cites revenue from 'buildings one and two', backs it. Judging the delay over March to June against the mid-2026 target is fair.

evidence.note: Bloomberg did report, and stood by, that Oracle and OpenAI were not going ahead with the planned expansion lease.
The dropped expansion was an extra 600MW near the campus, not the main eight-building site. This contradicts the 'past the initial two buildings' scope.
Crusoe disclosure from March 2025 setting mid-2026 for all eight buildings and 1.2 GW. This is the baseline target.
Epoch, citing an Oracle post, says about 200MW was operating on April 22, far short of 1.2 GW.
Oracle's June disclosure, via TNW, says 42% of Abilene capacity was delivered at the mid-2026 target date. That is well behind.
Oracle's denial says the rest of the site is on plan. Company statement; it also suggests buildings 3–8 were still being built for the existing tenant.

reviews.rationale: Two parts hold: Bloomberg reported that OpenAI and Oracle dropped the planned Abilene expansion, and the campus was far short of full energization by mid-2026 (about 200MW in April, 42% in June). His parenthetical is contradicted: the dropped expansion was an extra 600MW near the campus, not buildings three to eight, which were still under construction on the main site.

attribution.note: Zitron's own analytic sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: The 'may' covers only rates following prices. The scored conditional, 'if rates go up… will become significantly more expensive', is firm. The 'point or two' threshold is kept in original_threshold.

contract.note: Using the 10-year Treasury as the rate benchmark and AI borrowers' yields and spreads as the outcome is an ordinary reading. The contract flags that it cannot split rate-driven from credit-driven repricing.

evidence.note: Condition evidence: in September the Fed hiked, citing oil-driven inflation. This confirms prices and rates rose.
Condition evidence: the 10-year was up about a full point from its February low, which meets 'a point or two'.
July: the Meta El Paso financing was being discussed above 7%, about 0.4 points over the pre-war Hyperion deal. These were early terms.
October: blue-chip AI borrowers paid returns described as unthinkable before, with Meta above 7%. The article ties this to war-driven inflation.
Oracle's 5-year CDS went from 141 to 308bp during 2026, so its debt became more costly.
Puts part of the Meta repricing down to project-specific risk and deal supply. This weakens the rate-driven link but does not undo the cost rise.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent was met: oil-driven inflation, a Fed hike, and a 10-year yield up about a point (above 5.3% by October). After that, AI borrowers paid clearly more. Oracle's CDS more than doubled, and Meta-linked debt priced above 7%, higher than the pre-war Hyperion deal. This meets the early-resolution rule. One caveat: the sources also blame AI-specific risk, not only rates.

attribution.note: Zitron's own summarising sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: An unhedged forecast ('is about to'). Linking it to the energy, inflation and credit pressures matches the surrounding text.

contract.note: Reading 'world of hurt' as broad, substantial financial distress is ordinary. 'About to' sets no reproducible deadline, so leaving the horizon open is defensible, though it is lenient to the speaker.

evidence.note: Q3 2026: $102B went to AI startups, down from the prior quarter but high by historical standards. This weighs against broad distress but cannot settle an undated forecast.
Musk's view that debt markets shut to many neoclouds is a third party's opinion, and the financing details are uncertain. It is not an established industry-wide event.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no stated deadline. By the cutoff, the packet shows tightening credit and warnings, but also record-scale AI funding in Q3 2026. It shows no documented, broad AI-industry financial disruption tied to the stated pressures. The contract's support rule is not met and nothing can conclusively contradict the forecast, so it stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the antecedent ('if the debt spigot gets turned off'), his stated uncertainty ('we truly don't know', 'I do not think') and the full scope. The 'depends on debt' sentence is rhetorical and has no measure.

contract.note: Defining the antecedent as debt broadly becoming unavailable, not just pricier, is fair to his 'spigot gets turned off' wording.

evidence.note: Condition evidence: tech borrowing reached about $500B in nine months of 2026, so the spigot was not turned off.
Condition evidence: financing got costlier but the AI financing boom was not stalling, so the antecedent was not met.
By late October credit was tightening and crunch fears were rising, but debt supply had not shut down.

reviews.rationale: The checkable part is conditional on the debt spigot being turned off. The evidence shows debt kept flowing in large volumes, at higher cost, through October 2026, so the antecedent did not happen and the conditional is not scored. The forecast is also hedged ('we truly don't know', 'I do not think'), and the dependence-on-debt sentence is rhetorical with no measure.
